title: Now you remember dharma?
hookLine: Karna appeals to the rules of war, and Krishna answers with questions
carry: dharma is lived, not just claimed
tomorrow: after Karna, is it too late for peace?

cards: Wait. That's what Karna calls out, standing on the ground with his hands on the wheel. Wait, Arjuna.
A warrior in a chariot shouldn't strike a man who is on foot, whose wheel is stuck, who isn't ready. Those are the rules of fair fighting, he says, in effect. Remember dharma.
Give me a moment to free the wheel. By the rules the armies agreed to, it sounds like a fair request, made by a man in real trouble. And it isn't Arjuna who answers.
It's Krishna, from the driver's seat.

teach.b: Krishna's answer is a string of questions. Now you remember dharma, Karna? Where was it when Draupadi was dragged into the assembly hall and you mocked her?
At the rigged game of dice? When young Abhimanyu was surrounded by many warriors at once and cut down? And Krishna adds, in effect: people in trouble blame fate, never their own deeds.

In Ganguli's English, Karna hangs his head in shame, and says nothing. He climbs back into the stuck chariot and fights on. Then Arjuna, urged on by Krishna, takes up a single great arrow, and Karna falls.
The epic gives one more picture: a light rises from his body into the sun, his father. Here's what Hindus take from it.
Dharma isn't a rulebook you open only when you're losing. It's a way of living, and the life you've lived is what answers when you call on it.
Karna knew the rules of fair fighting perfectly; he just hadn't kept them for others. And notice the epic doesn't make him a cartoon villain.
Hindus still call him daanveer Karna, Karna the great giver, the man who gave away his own armor. Both are true, and the story holds both. One more thing.
The Pandavas, cheering, still don't know who just died. Kunti knows.
Her sons will learn after the war that they have killed their eldest brother.

how: Karna's death is retold in readings, regional theater, poems and serials, and Karna is discussed as a figure hard to judge: generous, loyal, wronged at birth, and complicit in wrong.

o: the son of the sun who dies fighting his unknowing brothers
the son of Drona, who fights on after the war is over
the charioteer's son who switches to the Pandava side

s: Karna answered Krishna with a long defense
he hung his head in shame and said nothing.
the epic paints Karna as a plain villain
Hindus still call him daanveer, the great giver; the story holds his gifts and his wrongs together.
Krishna's point: the dharma you call on must be dharma you've kept
he asked where Karna's dharma was when Draupadi was dragged into the hall.

games.q: a classmate who skipped every group meeting now says the grade split 'isn't fair' to him. by Krishna's answer to Karna, what fits?
o: ask him gently where fairness was during the meetings, and still hear him out.
split it evenly; fairness means everyone gets the same.
call him a fraud in front of the class.
games.why: Krishna didn't shout; he asked questions. dharma is a way of living, so the life you've lived answers when you call on it.

practice: Krishna made Karna look back at his own deeds. Sit quietly and let today replay: one moment you kept faith with someone, and one moment you didn't. Don't build a defense; let the quiet after it stay quiet.
If you pray, offer both moments to God in your own words. If you don't pray, just name them honestly to yourself.

wordCard.voice: Karna. The wheel stuck, the questions he couldn't answer, the light rising into the sun, and brothers who didn't yet know him.

orig.note: Karna: Kunti's firstborn son, raised in a charioteer's house, who died fighting his own brothers.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma is lived, not just claimed. Karna asked for a fairness he hadn't given. Day eight hundred forty-two, done.
